name: Hassan Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hassan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name never goes with your answers. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Oakfield Life, in the old building by the railway station, on the policy servicing team. That means the quiet middle of life insurance: people change address, add a new husband as the person who gets paid out, or want to know what their pension's worth. And the sad side, when someone dies and the family needs to claim. I've got my own little routine: coffee, the post tray, then the system queue till lunch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the sad side.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: When someone dies, the family sends the death certificate and the policy, and I check everything matches and start the payout. I talk to a lot of widows, and I'm better at that than at the system, to be honest. We moved to a new case system last year and I'm still the slowest on it; Ingrid, the supervisor, has had to sit with me more than once. I don't use any of the AI stuff, because I'd rather know what I've typed. I live with Sanne, my girlfriend, who teaches at a primary school, and we've saved over a year of costs toward a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. I've always said most of this was salesmen talking. At work I'd just say let's get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I can stop worrying and go back to worrying about the case system. Life insurance moves slowly; my firm still sends some letters by post. If AI shaves a few minutes off address changes, that's no skin off my nose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd keep going, keep putting money into the house fund every month, and maybe book a proper session with Ingrid to get faster on the case system. Sanne and I would probably buy next year, like we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit relieved. I like it when things stay roughly where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a few minutes off address changes. Is that a big part of your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a third, if I'm honest. Address changes, bank detail changes, name changes after weddings. If a program did all of those, I'd notice, but I'd still have the death claims and the phone calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the house you're saving for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small terraced house on the edge of town, near Sanne's school, with a garden for a dog one day. We've got the deposit nearly there. In a world where nothing much changes, we just buy it.

say: I'd say most of the AI talk was **salesmen talking**.
At work I'd just say let's **get on with it**.
think: Life insurance **moves slowly**, so a few saved minutes won't touch me much.
**Address changes** are a third of my day, but death claims and calls remain.
do: Keep paying into the **house fund** every month.
Book a session with Ingrid to get faster on the **case system**.
Buy the **terraced house** near Sanne's school next year.
feel: **Calm** and a bit **relieved** that things stay roughly put.
S0.quote: Life insurance moves slowly; my firm still sends some letters by post.
fieldNote: Hassan's calm comes from a **slow-moving employer** and a nearly complete house deposit.
He admits a **third of his day** is routine changes, but doesn't see that as a threat yet.
His real daily struggle is the **new case system**, not AI.

steps.text: Keep processing address changes and death claims at Oakfield Life
Keep paying into the house deposit every month
Buy the small terraced house near Sanne's school

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. I'm not going to be one of those people shouting about robots online. At work I'd say the firm should be sensible, bring things in slowly and look after people who've been loyal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job is the exact list you just read: checking, writing, answering customers. Policy servicing is what they'll automate first, because it's all forms. I'm junior, I'm slow on the system, and I don't touch the AI, so I'm not who they'll keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, that's my instinct, and probably hold off on the house for a year to see. I'd stay put and hope the death claims side needs people, because families don't want a machine when someone's died. If they offered training on the new tools, I'd go, but I wouldn't volunteer first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, in my stomach. I don't like change, and this is change I can't stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hold off on the house. What does Sanne say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say her job's safe and we can buy on her wage plus whatever I find. She's right on paper. But I don't want a mortgage the year I might lose my job, so we'd argue about it, quietly, like we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go to training but not volunteer. Why not volunteer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first people on a new system are the ones who find all the problems, and I'd be terrible at that. Let someone like Ingrid go first. I'd follow once it works.

say: I'd say **we'll see**, and stay off the internet about robots.
The firm should bring things in **slowly** and look after **loyal staff**.
think: **Policy servicing** is what they'll automate first, because it's all forms.
Being junior, slow and **AI-free**, I'm not who they'll keep.
do: Save harder and **delay the house** by a year.
Stay and hope the **death claims** side still needs people.
Attend **training** if offered, but not volunteer first.
feel: **Worried in his stomach** about change he can't stop.
S1.quote: Families don't want a machine when someone's died.
fieldNote: Hassan's public line is **wait and see**, but privately he expects to be cut.
He pins hope on **bereaved families** wanting a person, the part of the job he's good at.
A quiet **house disagreement** with his partner shows how caution shapes the household.

steps.text: Raise monthly savings and keep the deposit in cash
Put the house purchase off for a year
Wait to join AI training until colleagues prove it works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to slow this down, because two years is mad. People need time. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job's gone in two years, probably sooner. If a machine can do any thinking work, it can certainly change an address and check a death certificate. The only thing left would be talking to families, and I don't know if they'd pay me for that alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring my brother Karim, who fits heat pumps and boilers, and ask if he'd take me on as an apprentice. It's hands-on, so it buys about three years until 2031. I'd stay at Oakfield until they let me go, and keep every penny of the house money in the bank. The house wouldn't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. I'm not a person who likes starting over, and starting over at twenty-nine on an apprentice wage is not what I pictured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Karim when you rang?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm not good with my hands yet, but I turn up and I don't complain. He'd laugh, because when we were kids I wouldn't even change a bike tyre. Then he'd say yes, because he's my brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2031, when the robots come for hands-on work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've no idea. Maybe people will still want someone they know in their house fixing the heating. I can't plan past that, and I'm not going to pretend I can.

say: I'd say the **government** has to slow this down.
**Two years** is mad, and people need time to adjust.
think: My job is **gone in two years**, maybe sooner.
Only **talking to families** would remain, and I doubt they'd pay for that alone.
do: Ask his brother Karim for a **heat pump apprenticeship**.
Stay at Oakfield until laid off and **keep the deposit** in the bank.
feel: **Sick** at the idea of starting over.
**Unprepared** for a hands-on job he has never been good at.
S2.quote: I'm not a person who likes starting over, and starting over at twenty-nine on an apprentice wage is not what I pictured.
fieldNote: Hassan, normally cautious, jumps to a **hands-on fallback** when time runs out.
His brother's **heating firm** is his real safety net, more than the state.
He refuses to plan **beyond 2031**, which is honest rather than defeatist.

steps.text: Start a heat pump fitting apprenticeship with his brother Karim
Keep the whole house deposit in a savings account
Drop the plan to buy the terraced house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for firms to do this properly, with notice and retraining. And for the government to make sure they do. I'd still say it calmly; shouting doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job probably goes around 2030, but I've got a few years of wages first. I'm the type to sit tight too long, so honestly the risk is that I waste the five years. I know that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Oakfield, save hard, and start doing Saturdays with Karim from next year, just to see if I can stand it. If I can, I'd do the heating qualification part-time from 2028. And Sanne and I might buy a cheaper house, one we could pay on her wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less sick. Having Saturdays with Karim as a test makes it feel like something I can try rather than something that happens to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's a Saturday with Karim like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Up at six, freezing cold vans, crawling under old ladies' sinks. He talks the whole time. I'd probably hate it for a month and then quietly like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the risk is wasting the five years. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sanne, mostly. She'd put a date on the calendar and ask me about it every week. I need someone to do that, because left alone, I'd still be sorting the post tray at the insurance office in 2030.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough for firms to give notice and **retraining**.
The **government** should make sure firms actually do it.
think: My job probably **goes around 2030**, after a few more years of wages.
My real risk is that I **sit tight** and waste the five years.
do: Work **Saturdays with Karim** from next year as a test.
Start a part-time **heating qualification** from 2028 if it suits him.
Buy a **cheaper house** that Sanne's wage alone can cover.
feel: **Anxious** but less sick, because the Saturdays feel like a **trial** he controls.
S3.quote: Left alone, I'd still be sorting the post tray at the insurance office in 2030.
fieldNote: Five years gives Hassan a **low-risk test**: Saturdays on his brother's vans.
He openly knows his **tendency to wait** and relies on his partner to set dates.
He'd still buy a house, but one sized to **one wage**.

steps.text: Keep working at Oakfield Life while saving hard
Work Saturdays on Karim's heating vans from next year
Start a part-time heating qualification in 2028
Buy a cheaper house that Sanne's wage can cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's not panic. Firms and government should plan it out sensibly, and people should have time to retrain. I'd probably be the voice of calm at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time in my head. I'd be 37 when the thinking AI comes. I worry I'd use all ten years telling myself there's still time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Oakfield, buy the house with Sanne, and keep saving. I'd ask Ingrid about moving to the death claims team, because that's the bit with people in it. Then maybe in 2030 I'd start the heating training with Karim properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. It's like knowing the car needs new tyres eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the death claims team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the part of the job where a person on the phone matters most. A woman ringing about her late husband's policy doesn't want a chatbot. If anything in insurance keeps people the longest, it's that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell yourself at 37, looking back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopefully that I started the heating course on time. Knowing me, I'd be telling myself I should have started two years earlier.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty, so let's not panic.
Firms and government should **plan sensibly** and give people time to retrain.
think: I'd be **37** when thinking AI arrives.
I worry I'd spend all ten years telling myself there's **still time**.
do: Buy the **house** with Sanne and keep saving.
Ask Ingrid about moving to the **death claims team**.
Start **heating training** with Karim properly around 2030.
feel: **Uneasy in the background**, like knowing the car will need new tyres.
S4.quote: A woman ringing about her late husband's policy doesn't want a chatbot.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Hassan stay **comfortable**, which he sees as both a gift and a trap.
He looks for the **most human corner** of insurance, death claims, to last longest.
The heating plan stays, but is **pushed back** to 2030.

steps.text: Buy the terraced house with Sanne next year
Ask Ingrid for a move to the death claims team
Start heating engineer training with Karim around 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is no time for someone like me, who needs a year just to get used to a new computer system. What would help is a rule that firms give real notice, maybe a year, and some help paying for apprenticeships when you're not eighteen any more.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the families who ring in. When someone's husband dies, the life insurance policy is often the only thing in the house that's organised. I'd like to think a person will still be there to explain it.

headlineQuote: When someone's husband dies, the life insurance policy is often the only thing in the house that's organised.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old life policy clerk** at an old insurer, slow on the new case system.
He avoids AI tools, likes **routine**, and is good with **bereaved families**.
He and his partner Sanne, a teacher, have **over a year** saved toward a house.
His fallback is an **apprenticeship** at his brother Karim's heating firm.
He is **calm** if nothing changes and **alarmed** if AGI arrives in two years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he needs a year just to adjust to a new computer system.
whatWouldHelp: A rule giving **a year's notice** before AI job cuts.
Help paying for **apprenticeships** for adults who aren't eighteen any more.
